signals.headline: Debt-free, net investor by £93.670m, all treasury figures reconcile — including a zero-on-zero PWLB match
signals.why_it_matters: Nothing alarms in the paper. The strategy is well-structured, the mid-year Table 6 discloses every deposit at loan level, and the balance-sheet identity ties at every year and at the mid-year point. The single strategic change (LA maturity 1yr → 2yr) is clearly flagged and explained. This is a 'verified quiet' record — worth having in the library specifically because most of what we read is borrowers under stress.

signals.headline: Not a borrowing increase — a LENDING increase: LA line up from £23m/29% to £53m/56% in six months
signals.why_it_matters: The Council doubled its inter-authority lending in half a year and now proposes to extend the maximum tenor from 1 year to 2 years. Second half of the same strategic decision. Worth flagging because we track the LA borrowing market across the library and Mid Sussex is now materially on the OTHER side of it.

summary.text:
Mid Sussex is a small district that is genuinely debt-free. PWLB principal is £0.000m at both 31.03.25 and 30.09.25 (Table 4 p.9); the mid-year report states outright that 'the PWLB borrowing was fully repaid in 2022/23' (mid-year para 29 p.35). The only debt on the balance sheet is one 2018 finance lease, running off from £1.069m (31.03.25) to £0.913m (30.09.25) to zero by 2028/29. Our loan file returns no PWLB entries for Mid Sussex — zero on zero, the strongest reconciliation the loan book can offer for a council in this position. The balance-sheet identity (CFR minus borrowing minus other long-term liabilities equals internal borrowing) ties at every year in Table 5 and at the mid-year point in Table 3 mid-year.

The interesting thing is what has happened on the investment side. Local authority lending was £23m / 29% of the book at 31.03.25 and £53m / 56% at 30.09.25 — more than doubled in six months, and now by a wide margin the largest single sector. Mid-year Table 6 (p.41) lists every deposit loan-by-loan: 14 LAs and PCCs at rates 4.15% (South Tyneside) to 5.25% (Highland), weighted 4.44%. Three of them — Manchester City £5m@4.50%, Highland £2m@5.25%, Police & Crime Lancashire £5m@4.95% — mature in December 2025, £12m rolling at a weighted 4.86%. Recommendation (iii) proposes extending the maximum LA investment period from 1 year to 2 years (para 20.11 p.13); read together with the doubling, that reads as a single strategic decision — increase LA allocation and extend duration into a falling-curve expectation (MUFG forecast Bank Rate 3.50% by Sep-26, mid-year p.34).

The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is NEGATIVE across the entire horizon (Annex A p.30): -18.2%, -16.5%, -13.5%, [likely -]11.7%, -9.9%. Treasury is a net contributor to the General Fund rather than a cost line — the £86.4m average investment balance (mid-year para 51) is doing that work. The liability benchmark is quite properly OMITTED under para 9.1 ('required for authorities that have a borrowing need but since Mid Sussex Council is debt free the Liability Benchmark has been omitted'). Investment income Q2 25/26 was £1.8m net (mid-year para 53). Report authored under a shared service with Adur & Worthing (SSA since October 2010, SLA extended three years from October 2025); advisor MUFG, bank Lloyds. Draft written and machine-checked; ready to send.

officer.body:
Hi Rachel,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO curve, and a training academy for officers and members. More — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the TMSS and Mid-Year Report that went to Council on 10 December. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your mid-year Table 6 lists every deposit loan-by-loan and the balance-sheet arithmetic ties at every year, which is not the norm across the library, and this is offered in that spirit.

A cross-check first, which comes out cleanly. Our loan file returns no PWLB entries for Mid Sussex, and the paper agrees — paragraph 29 of the mid-year states outright that the PWLB was fully repaid in 2022/23, and Table 4 prints £0.000m at both 31 March 2025 and 30 September 2025. Zero on zero is the strongest reconciliation the loan book can offer for a council in your position. The Table 5 balance-sheet identity ties at every year, and it also ties at the mid-year point: £5.101m CFR less zero borrowing less £0.913m of lease equals your £4.188m of internal borrowing.

The interesting thing is what has happened on the other side. Local authority lending was £23m of the £79.815m book at 31 March 2025, 29%. Six months later it was £53m of £94.583m, 56%. In half a year the LA line has doubled in cash and jumped 27 percentage points as a share, and it is now by a wide margin the largest single sector you carry. Recommendation (iii) proposes extending the maximum tenor from one year to two. Those two decisions read as a single strategic move — increase the LA allocation and take the curve at longer duration — and it's the kind of move a sector-wide view is genuinely useful for. We track what councils are actually paying and offering on the LA market across the library, so where your counterparties are pricing money at one, three, six, twelve and now twenty-four months is visible rather than inferred. That sits alongside the PWLB borrowing side at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One near-term point from your Table 6. Three of your LA deposits mature between 1 December and 18 December — Manchester City £5m at 4.50%, Highland £2m at 5.25% and Lancashire PCC £5m at 4.95% — £12m at a weighted 4.86%. Your own MUFG forecast on mid-year page 34 had Bank Rate falling from 4.00% at September 2025 to 3.50% by September 2026, and the 5-year PWLB certainty rate from 4.80% to 4.30% over the same window. Whatever those three roll into prices against a curve closer to the lower end of that path than to where the originals were struck, and December is a thin month for the LA market. Peer context is worth having before the roll rather than after it. The live pathway sits alongside CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

One last thing the paper does that most don't. Your Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream in Annex A runs negative across the whole horizon — minus 18.2% for 2024/25 through minus 9.9% for 2028/29. Investment income exceeds debt-service, so treasury is a net contributor to the General Fund rather than a cost line, on the £86.4m of average balances you cite in mid-year paragraph 51. Very few of the councils we've read sit that way, and the sector narrative tends to assume the ratio is positive — worth having the peer context for if the topic ever comes up with members.

On training, four fit. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets is the most directly relevant given the shape of your book and the maturity change. Investment strategy for debt-free councils is written for exactly the position you're in. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where CIPFA is heading with the codes, even though paragraph 9.1 quite properly omits it from your indicators. And Members' introduction to treasury is written for the annual strategy cycle. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
